newsitem.title: USA: Russia's crown jewels head for Houston-officials.
newsitem.headline: Russia's crown jewels head for Houston-officials.

text.p: Treasures of Russia's imperial past finally headed for a Houston museum on Friday but the rest of a planned American tour was still to be settled, Russian and U.S. officials said.

"We're on the road to Houston and hopefully beyond," said James Symington, whose American-Russian Cultural Cooperation Foundation helped set up the U.S. tour and negotiated the end to a weeks-long wrangle after Russia said it wanted the treasures back.

The visible symbol of the disagreement, a huge moving van packed with jewel-encrusted costumes, icons, portraits and other artifacts, rolled out of the gated Russian embassy compound in Washington on Friday afternoon. It had been there since Monday. Next stop is the Houston Museum of Fine Arts.

That followed nearly two weeks when the van was blocked by Russian diplomats' cars at the curb outside the Corcoran Museum of Art in Washington, where a popular exhibit called "Jewels of the Romanovs" closed on April 13. Some 80,000 people saw the show at $9 per person during the 10-week run.
Russian officials said then that materials from the exhibit, notably Russia's crown jewels, should be returned to Moscow for the celebration of the 850th anniversary of the city's founding.

But on Friday, Mikhael Gusman, executive director of the Russian Organising Committee for the treasures, said agreement had been reached to send the collection on to Houston where the exhibit was expected to open on schedule on May 11.

Asked by reporters outside the embassy gates whether the show would proceed as planned to San Diego, California and Memphis, Tennessee, Gusman said, "According to the agreement (Houston) has to be the last place in the United States, but both sides hope on further negotiations on this."

Neither Gusman nor Symington would say if Russia would make more money under Friday's agreement as opposed to the original contract, but Symington acknowledged that Russia would get a share of the proceeds of the travelling show.
Asked whether the Russians' share would increase, Symington replied, "I would say that they're probably in a better position now than they were before in that respect."

"This was not about money, this was about the very important patrimony of the Russian Federation," Timothy Dickinson, a lawyer for Russia in this matter, told reporters. "The Russian Federation has significant issues with respect to the treatment of the exhibit, the security of these invaluable properties and money was a secondary factor."
Negotiations to determine whether the exhibit will continue on to San Diego and Memphis, and possibly other cities as well, will begin soon, Symington said.
The original schedule called for the show to open in San Diego on August 16 and in Memphis on November 20.
The exhibition was timed to commemorate the U.S. visit 125 years ago of Grand Duke Alexis. The Romanovs ruled Russia for 300 years, ending in the 1917 Communist revolution.
